scenes.visual: Title card: Semaphorins: Keeping Axons on Course. Show an axon turning away from a shaded inappropriate territory.

scenes.tts: Semaphorins guide growing axons by repelling their growth cones from places they must not enter. Keeping axons out of the wrong territory helps them reach the right place. In the spinal cord, Sema three A helps keep pain fibres out of the ventral horn, while muscle-stretch fibres enter. Other cues probably share this work. A growth cone is the spread fan at an axon tip. In a dish, a repellent can fold that fan into a thin tip. That is collapse.

scenes.visual: Open on a developing sensory pathway in a spinal cord cross-section. Yellow Sema3A in the ventral cord repels teal pain-fibre growth cones; pain fibres terminate dorsally while a separately labelled muscle afferent enters the ventral horn. Label Sema3A as one of the cues involved. Zoom to a spread growth cone, then transition to an explicitly labelled dish assay where the fan folds into a thin tip. Omit purification, collapsin naming and potency graphics.

scenes.tts: How does the growth cone hear Sema three A? This secreted semaphorin binds neuropilin tightly. But neuropilin has only a short tail inside the cell, with nothing that looks like an enzyme. A receptor that catches a signal must also pass it on. Where is the wire?

scenes.visual: Zoom from the growth cone to its membrane. Yellow Sema3A docks on blue neuropilin. Show the short intracellular tail and the question: where is the wire? Remove independent-discovery and numerical tail-length labels.
scenes.narration: How does the growth cone hear Sema3A? This secreted semaphorin binds neuropilin tightly. But neuropilin has only a short tail inside the cell, with nothing that looks like an enzyme. A receptor that catches a signal must also pass it on. Where is the wire?

scenes.tts: The answer is plexin. In engineered cells, neither protein alone let Sema three A shrink the cell. Together, they did. Most class three semaphorins reach plexins through neuropilin. Membrane semaphorins can bind plexins directly. Neuropilin catches. Plexin signals.

scenes.visual: Show neuropilin alone and plexin alone with no shrinking, then their paired complex with shrinking, explicitly in engineered cells. Follow with two receptor diagrams: most secreted class 3 cues use neuropilin and plexin; membrane semaphorins can meet plexin directly. Label neuropilin catches and plexin signals.

scenes.tts: Other work split the jobs. A neuropilin without its tail still supported collapse. A plexin stripped of its inner part blocked Sema three A responses in sensory neurons. So neuropilin catches. Plexin signals.
scenes.caption: Other work split the jobs. A neuropilin without its tail still supported collapse. A plexin stripped of its inner part blocked Sema3A responses in sensory neurons. So neuropilin catches. Plexin signals.
scenes.visual: Retain the deletion comparison: remove the neuropilin tail and show collapse still occurs; reset, remove the plexin intracellular part and show the Sema3A response blocked in sensory neurons. Finish with catches and signals labels.
scenes.narration: Other work split the jobs. A neuropilin without its tail still supported collapse. A plexin stripped of its inner part blocked Sema3A responses in sensory neurons. So neuropilin catches. Plexin signals.

scenes.tts: Inside the cell, plexin has a domain that acts as a G A P. It speeds G T P hydrolysis and switches a small G T Pase off. This can lower integrin adhesion. Plexin signalling also engages Rho family G T Pases and proteins that act on actin and microtubules.
scenes.caption: Inside the cell, plexin has a domain that acts as a GAP. It speeds GTP hydrolysis and switches a small GTPase off. This can lower integrin adhesion. Plexin signalling also engages Rho family GTPases and proteins that act on actin and microtubules.
scenes.visual: Show the plexin intracellular GAP domain speeding a small GTPase from its GTP-bound state to its off state, followed by reduced integrin adhesion. Use a generic small-GTPase label; remove the Plexin-B1 and R-Ras/Rap history. Beside this pathway, show plexin signalling engaging Rho-family GTPases and effectors acting on actin and microtubules.
scenes.narration: Inside the cell, plexin has a domain that acts as a GAP. It speeds GTP hydrolysis and switches a small GTPase off. This can lower integrin adhesion. Plexin signalling also engages Rho family GTPases and proteins that act on actin and microtubules.

scenes.tts: The net result is local loss of actin and adhesion. On one side of a growth cone, that means a turn. Everywhere at once, it means collapse. This connects the receptor signal to a change in direction.
scenes.caption: The net result is local loss of actin and adhesion. On one side of a growth cone, that means a turn. Everywhere at once, it means collapse. This connects the receptor signal to a change in direction.
scenes.visual: Show local actin and adhesion loss on one side of the growth cone and a turn away. Reset and show loss all around the fan, producing collapse. Visually connect cue, receptor complex, intracellular change and turning.
scenes.narration: The net result is local loss of actin and adhesion. On one side of a growth cone, that means a turn. Everywhere at once, it means collapse. This connects the receptor signal to a change in direction.

scenes.tts: The response also depends on the receiving cell. In the developing cortex, Sema three A repels a pyramidal neuron's axon but attracts its apical dendrite. The same cue can give different answers. Keep the purpose in view: semaphorin signals help growing axons avoid the wrong territories and build the right pathways.
scenes.visual: Show a developing cortical pyramidal neuron below the pial surface, with Sema3A high near the surface. Label the axon growing away and the apical dendrite growing toward the cue. Then return to the opening spinal pathway and end on semaphorins helping axons avoid inappropriate territories. Do not show a universal attraction/repulsion switch.
